utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, you can bring in the witness, but we should perhaps first have the blinds pulled up. I should like to thank you, the interpreters, for having helped me with the text. We managed to clarify the issue together, and thank you very much. As far as I can see, Mr. Waidyaratne is going to examine the witness. Do we have a summary of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have handed over the summary to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't think that the Judges have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It could be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think that the principle of equality should also be guaranteed for the Judges as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm a little hesitant after yesterday's events, but I would once again raise the question. I believe this time that the witness would be willing to continue, that the issue of a possible extended day to finish this witness today, since we are coming up on a weekend, so that we could finish. We believe the direct will be completed before the end of the normal day, and so, therefore, it would only be the cross-examination that would need to go beyond, if it's at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but there we seem to have a problem. Things are a little complicated. I do not dare ask anybody, on a Friday afternoon, to continue work, and that's the first point. Secondly, people have different engagements. The Judges have their own agenda and engagements. So that is not possible unless, unless we restrict -- that is to say, the Judges, the Chamber, can be complete until 2.30. However, two Judges could go on until 3.00. I, myself, can stay until midnight if need be, as far as I'm concerned, but I think that this -- that the situation is as it stands. We can resort to Rule 15, but only for half an hour, and I don't think it would really be convenient or advisable. We do understand. We fully understand the position. However, I think we're going to have to -- that is to say, unless we try and do our best to get through the examination-in-chief and cross-examination by 2.30. That would be wonderful. So let's try. Let's all try. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Waidyaratne, who is the man standing up to your right. Is the witness going to testify in public, with the use of a pseudonym? Is that right? So Witness, would you please take a look at the piece of paper that the usher is going to show you, and tell us whether your name is on that piece of paper. I apologise, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to have interrupted you. The witness will testify under her name, not under a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So that was a little confusion on my part, but the OTP led me to conclude that it would be Witness O. So that was a slight confusion on my part. Never mind. Go ahead, Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, could you kindly state your name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could the witness repeat her name, please.

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Nedzija Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell the Court your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of September, 1956, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: My ethnicity is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you residing until July 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Until July 1992, I lived in Prijedor, at Pecani. The street was Ratko Bujevic Coca, number G1, flat number 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I am married, and my husband's name is Fehim Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you have children by that marriage?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I have two children. They are 14 and 19 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you employed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I worked in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you start work?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I started work in 1976, working in the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then when did you start working in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: In 1981, I started working in the intermunicipal SUP. Afterwards, I moved to the traffic police department of Prijedor for traffic security, which belonged to the security centre of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was the head of the department or section that you worked?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: The traffic police? His name was Fikret Kadirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you work for any other person thereafter or was there any other head that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I also worked for the chief of SUP, that is to say, of the secretariat, and his name was Hasan Talundzic, because his secretary was on sick leave. So I replaced her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you start work for Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I started working for Hasan Talundzic -- that is to say, I don't remember the exact date. Nevenka Sikman and I would take turns working for him, but this was after the SDA party had come into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your work related to? What were the functions that you performed under Fikret Kadirevic and thereafter under Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Well, I did administration work in the police department, and I would see to the paper work when requests came in and everything else, anything that had to be typed out and so on. So it was administrative work mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, did you come into contact with the police personnel or police officers from other areas?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I was in contact with everybody working in the SUP building. I would often go across the hallway to the other police -- traffic police department in Prijedor. I would meet my colleagues there. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you stop work?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I stopped work the day when they took me to the camp, on the 23rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, did you sign a loyalty oath, loyalty to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign a loyalty oath saying that I would work and respect the laws that they enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When was this, and in front of whom did you sign this oath?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when I signed the loyalty oath, but it was after the takeover of power by the SDS; that is to say, when they took over the SUP building. I went to work, and Mira the secretary was present, and she told me that we should all go on holiday and think about whether we were going to sign the loyalty oath or not. Seven days later, I went to the SUP and signed this loyalty oath paper and continued to work in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In front of whom did you sign this oath?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I signed the loyalty oath in the office of the chief of SUP, Mr. Simo Drljaca, in the presence of Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was Simo present that day?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Drljaca was in the office when I was handed the loyalty oath -- or rather, the piece of paper that I had to sign to pledge my loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why did you sign this oath?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I signed the piece of paper so that I could continue working and keep my family. And I wasn't much bothered about who my superiors were because I thought that everything would continue just as it had done up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did anyone from your own ethnicity or from any of the Muslims force you not to take this oath or ask you not to take this oath?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No, nobody forced me not to sign it, but I just thought about it. We thought about it, whether I should, whether I shouldn't, and then I, myself, decided to sign the loyalty oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Especially after the taking of the power by the Serbs and also when this oath was taken, could you explain as to what prevailed within the employees of the police station or the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: In the SUP, people of Serb ethnicity were prevalent. They worked in their offices, and I ended up by working in the canteen and handing out meals to people I didn't know who came to the SUP. That's where I ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you were not working in the office as earlier, but you were put to the canteen to attend to other matters in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was sitting in the office without having anything to do, whereas my colleague Nevenka Sikman had so much work to do she couldn't even have a break, but -- so they sent me to wash dishes, distribute meals to people who worked in the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, who were the people who were present in the places that you were working?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: They were Serbs. They were workers who had worked there before with us, with me. Fellow employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any other non-Serbs working with you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No, I was alone. And there was another colleague of mine, her name was Hasna Ceric. She had also signed the loyalty oath, and she worked in the passport department issuing passports on the ground floor. The two of us didn't have any contact, though. We didn't meet in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to the people whom you worked with, people like the chief, Fikret Kadirevic, and Hasan Talundzic, do you know what happened to them after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I no longer saw them. I heard from Radenko Stakic that the chief had been arrested, that he had been taken to prison; whereas Talundzic, I didn't see him either, but I heard later on, on the radio that he had disappeared, that they were looking for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear about an attack on Prijedor during this time?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that there had allegedly been an attack on Prijedor. I heard that when I came to work in the morning. And when I went into my office, Nevenka Sikman was there. And Radenko Stakic was there, and he told me that there had been an attack of some kind. But Mira came and then told me that I ought to go on leave, to have a bit of a rest, a bit of a holiday, and to think about what I was going to do in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What happened thereafter? Did you know as to what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: When the attack on Prijedor took place, the following day, that is to say, two days I wasn't able to leave my apartment because the Muslims were not allowed to leave their homes. And it was only on the second day that I managed to go down to the ground floor of our building, and I saw a police car. And my friend, Vladimir Sobot, who worked in my police station came by, and he asked me about my family because he knew that I lived close by. And I said that I didn't know where my family were, and he said he could help me and take me to the technical centre school where all the locals from the old part of town had been put up. I went off with him, but he said that I wasn't safe walking around with him so that he would take me home, and that they had probably been taken to the Trnopolje camp. So I returned to in front of my building and then went towards my mother's house on foot. I didn't find anybody there; the house had been burnt. So that I heard some voices and came upon my brother who said that he had put my -- our mother up in a neighbour's house. I went and got my mother back, brought her back to my apartment, went to SUP on the third day, and then heard Radenko say that there had been an attack on Prijedor, and I saw that the windows had been shattered. Some of our windows in the building had been shattered as well. Is that what you wanted to hear? Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that we should focus on the essential points --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because even if we do our best, we're not going to complete the examination of this witness if we let the witness recount things on her own. So it's up to you to guide the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't want to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, was your husband with you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, he was. My husband was with us in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. On the 2nd of July, a policeman, Strika, came by with a reserve policeman, and he said that he was on a list and was to be taken to the Omarska camp. He was taken to SUP, and Strika told me on that occasion that my husband -- as I was an employee of SUP, perhaps I could help my husband and that I should go and see if I could help him. And I went off, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know where your husband was taken subsequently, or where he was held?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the SUP. He hadn't arrived yet. The van which came to collect my husband went around Prijedor to collect other people as well, and some 60 minutes later, after I had arrived in the SUP building, I saw him being brought into the SUP. And I asked Dusan Jankovic to help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, I apologise for interrupting again, but I see that the transcript did not translate what I said. I don't mind you allowing the witness to continue, but I think that the Prosecutor should always guide matters so that they focus on the essential. The fact that we're leaving the witness speak freely on her personal facts and how she was arrested, that is a good way of going speedily ahead, too. So we should go ahead, proceed with speed, but focus on the essential. So I don't mind the fact that you allowed the witness to express herself; that is fine. But the Prosecutor should move from personal data and the time of her arrest to Omarska. That is where we want to get to, but I leave that up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'll try my best, Your Honour. You will see that it was a direct question that I asked with regard to the husband and where he was held last which could have been answered with one. I'm sorry. I will try my best, and I will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, my question was, did you know that your husband was detained in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My husband was taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Answer my question with -- when I ask you a specific question with "yes" or "no," please. If you need to make -- give an explanation, you could do thereafter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, my husband was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to send any parcels or packages to him?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you send any food to him, and through whom?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I sent food through a colleague of mine, Nada Markovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you able to speak to Nada, and did she ever tell you about the situation in the camp or as to the people who were held there?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to Nada, and Nada said that they were having a nice time there; but then she told me that I should get some clothing to my husband. And then the food that she took was reduced to one -- to a sandwich.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this Nada you mentioned, who was she, and what ethnicity did she belong to?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Nada was a Serb, and she worked as a typist in the crime department of the SUP in Prijedor. She took down the minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did she --

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: -- in Omarska in the camp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did she say anything about the people who were in authority in the camp, to you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion she told me that they had some groups, and that my Fehim was in the third group. And she said that she wasn't taking the parcels herself to my husband but that Krkan was helping her, that he was giving my husband the parcels that I had sent to him through her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did she tell you as to who was in authority in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: She just told me that as she couldn't reach the prisoners, that the shift leader Krkan, that she had given the shift leader Krkan the food to take to my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Nedzija, you were arrested subsequently?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I was arrested on the 23rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who came and informed you, and who spoke to you with regard to your arrest?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Bato Kovacevic talked to me. He waited for me in front of my building and said he had an arrest warrant to take me to Omarska. As he knew me, we worked in the same building, he said, "Nedzija, I don't want them to arrest you, so you come up and report there yourself," which is what I, in fact, did do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you go to the police station or the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: First of all, I went to my apartment and left the things that I had bought. I took my children and went off with my children because I thought the chief, Simo, would not take me to the camp when he saw me with my two children, that he would have pity on me. But when I got there, I found that the situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you able to speak to Simo?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: When I arrived at the SUP, I went into the office of Mira Topic first of all. She was Simo Drljaca's secretary. And then they came to fetch me and said that I should go to the camp. And she laughed, she always had this sort of artificial smile, and said, "Nedzija, it's not anything terrible. You'll just make a statement and come back. And Simo Drljaca is busy. You can't go into his office." But I didn't listen to her. I went into Simo Drljaca's office myself, and he was sitting at his table, and I addressed him by saying, "Chief, please don't take me to the camp. Allow me to remain in house arrest. I have small children and a sick mother at home." And he said, "It's wartime," he could do nothing about it, and that I had to go to the camp. I cried and I entreated him, pleaded with him, but he got up from the table and said he was in a hurry, off somewhere. I went down the corridor with him. And my husband's brother turned up, and he was good friends with Simo Drljaca, they knew each other, and he said, "Simo, don't take my sister-in-law off. Take me, I'm a man. You took off my brother. Take me too." And he said that he couldn't do anything, and he just left into the -- went into the courtyard. So that then I went home, and Ranko Gvozden, he was on the service on duty there, he said that I should take my children home and return. I went home, took up my belongings, some things that I needed, and returned to the SUP. And he said that I should sit down on the bench and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you subsequently taken to any -- taken away from the SUP?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I sat there for perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the others who were taken with you, and how did they take you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: When they called me to come out into the courtyard, I went into the car. Sead Pasic, the deputy, Fikret Kadirevic, and Alija Jakupovic were already in the car. This second one was a neighbour whom I knew from before, and then a woman and two men were brought along, and later on I heard that that was the woman who worked in the Crvena Ruza or Red Roses. Her name was Sabiha, I think. Whether she was with her brother or husband, I don't know, but we left the SUP courtyard after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know the ethnicity of these people who were with you then?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. They were all Muslims like me, all of them in the car with me, in the van with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This van, did it go to any -- stop on the way?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. We went on for a short time and then the van stopped. I heard a noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And where did it stop?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: The van stopped in front of the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did anybody get into the van or was put into the van then?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Four people got into the van. I knew one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: That was the PE teacher, what Mustafa Habibovic and three other people that I didn't know. And they all sat on our laps because there wasn't enough room for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was their condition? Did you see them? Did you speak to them? Could you explain to the Court as to what you saw and what was the condition of these people who got into the van?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: They were in a pitiful state. They were hungry. They were thin. They had shown -- they showed us their hands, and you could see the signs of cigarettes butts which had been extinguished on the palms of their hands. I had taken some food with me to take to my husband, and I took pity on them, so I gave them some food to eat. They were pitiful to look at. They had been beaten up. They stank because they were in that condition. And you could see that they had suffered a lot, and they showed me the burns on the palms of their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you finally arrive at?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I arrived at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you asked to get down from the van? And what happened to the others who were there with you in the van?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. The van stopped, the door opened, the men got out first, the ones who had come in last, and they separated the men straight away, made them stand up against the wall of the building and they had to place their hands behind their heads on their necks. I went out then and some of them were standing around. I saw Zeljko Meakic first. He was standing there, and next to him there were two or three others, other policemen whom I didn't know. When they saw me, they began laughing and saying, "Look what this one looks like. We don't know if she's white or black or whatever." I don't know what I looked like when I got out of the van. I must have looked awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Meakic say anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. Meakic said, "Leave her alone. Don't touch her. Take her into the restaurant, through the kitchen door, with the other women," and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I was taken to the restaurant at that point. I passed through the kitchen and ended up in the restaurant where a group of women was. I saw also the detainees who were eating and the other group who was about to leave the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be a convenient time to adjourn, to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a convenient time indeed. However, during the break, I should like the parties to consider the idea of having two Judges hearing the witness so that we can finish her testimony. As I said, we could go for another half hour, but only two Judges. Let me ask the usher to help the witness out of the courtroom. We can perhaps have a shorter break. However, the accused need enough time to leave the courtroom and come back. I think that we must have a half-hour break if the accused are to be taken out of the courtroom. Half hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Keegan, do you have any news, any good news, regarding our going until 3.00 this afternoon, bearing in mind the conditions that I have proposed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just after we recess, Your Honour, I spoke with some members of the Defence. We indicated we think that it would be about another 30, 35 minutes of direct. It was unclear at that time whether Defence knew whether an additional hour would be sufficient to complete cross, so I really have to pass it to my colleagues to determine -- to find out if they've determined how long they need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the response of the Defence to your first question, whether we agree to go on with hearing the witness in the presence of two Judges, the answer is positive: Yes, we fully agree with that proposal. As regards the issue of the time that we need, whether we can complete the examination within one hour, we would like to see the end of the examination-in-chief because it is very difficult for us at this point to tell you how long our cross-examination will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then, we will have to wait, and we will wait. But let me ask the Prosecutor once again to make an additional effort with that objective in mind. Let us please speed up things. Mr. Usher, can you bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Waidyaratne, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, before the adjournment you spoke about your arrival in the Omarska camp. After your arrival, did you meet the person whom you referred to as Zeljko Meakic in the evening?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And were you, were you able to meet with your husband that evening?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you meet your husband?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: We met in the corridor above the stairway near the entrance to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this person whom you said -- referred to as Meakic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic was the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know him previously?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is he the one who arranged the meeting with your husband?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long were you able to be with your husband?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: For about 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thereafter, were you called out by anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: It was Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How did it happen? Where did he come to?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: He came to our room where we were supposed to spend the night, and he said, "Nedzija, come with me to the room, to my office," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you go to -- did you follow him?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you go to, and what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: He went to his office, and at that point he told me, "Nedzija, I'm a shift leader, and I have to take down your personal details."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what else did he say? Did he advise you on anything?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion he told me, "Well, Nedzija, you know there are several women here. Some of them are dangerous. Those who had been arrested with weapons, you should not have contact with them very often," and he sort of counselled me on how I should behave in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know this person before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him. He used to work at the station in Ljubija, so I would see him when he would come to the main SUP building in Prijedor. Also, I would see him in passing, or during the meetings with my colleague, Mevlida in the office. I used to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I didn't know his real name. I knew him by his nickname Krkan and by his surname Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After he advised you, did you go back to your room?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I went back to my room after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How was he dressed when you met him that time?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform. I think that the shirt was blue in colour with short sleeves, and a pair of trousers. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, it was a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that he took you to a room. Where was this room? Which floor?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: The room was right across from our room; that is, the room where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was there anybody present at that time in that room?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No, only Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you, during your stay or your detention in the camp, did you see the normal guards using that room?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No. I didn't see guards upstairs, I mean, the regular guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the people who were using that room? Did you see as to who used that room?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: The room was used by Krkan and other regular policemen, together with Zeljko Meakic and another man whose name I cannot remember, but I know he used to work in the SUP, at the crime department and that he was retired. But I really cannot remember his name or his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give a description of this person when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question. Which person?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said, "Another man whose name I cannot remember, but I know he used to work in the SUP, at the crime department."

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think that I could recognise him because I remember the individual very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that he was retired. Did you know, in the crime department, what his position was?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. His position was, I think, that of an inspector, and he used to work at the same office as Reuf Travancic. Something to do with fire prevention. I'm not sure. I used to see him in that office, and I think that the two of them were colleagues, worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During the day when you were in detention, where did you spend your time?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: We would spend the time in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you asked to do any work?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: I helped in the kitchen. I helped with the dishes and the distribution of the food from time to time. I would bring bread and things like that. The women who were there had been doing that kind of work for a while, and when I came, I joined them in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: We slept in the upstairs area, in the offices upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the offices"? Did you know as to whether these rooms were used for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. They were offices of the investigators who would come during the day to interrogate the detainees. And after they would leave, we would clean up the office and sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you clean the rooms? You said that you all would clean the rooms. Did you clean the rooms during your detention?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I helped my friends there to clean the area, and then we would put down the mattresses so we could sit down or lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you observe anything when you cleaned these rooms?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, we did. There would be smashed chairs on the floor, whips. On one particular occasion we found a pair of spectacles that had been broken. Blood would be on the floor. We had to wash the floor in order to remove those stains and not to have to look at it. There were all kinds of metal objects, pieces of wire, kinds of whips with extensions on them, and we would remove those objects and put them on one of the shelves that were in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During your detention, did you observe anybody going up to these rooms in the daytime, other than the interrogators that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I saw detainees being taken upstairs for interrogation. I would usually see two guards taking one detainee upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see them coming back afterwards?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes, I would see them coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see as to what their condition was or as to how they looked had they were returning?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. Usually they would go for interrogation in a normal way. They would walk in a normal way. However, on the way back, they could hardly walk. Very often they would have to be carried because they were unable to walk because of the beatings they had sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see, at any time, a person by the name of Reuf Travancic when you were in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I saw Reuf Travancic. He happened to have strayed in the restaurant by mistake. He was in a very bad condition. He had been badly beaten up. His back was all bruised from whippings. He normally wore glasses but he had no glasses on him on that occasion. So he was walking around. He looked terrible. And at the end, a guard took him by his hand and led him out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before we leave that area, you mentioned about seeing interrogators coming into the Omarska camp and going into these rooms. Who were these interrogators? Did you know anybody by name?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. They came in the morning around half past seven, in a small bus. They were mainly employees of the SUP in Prijedor, but there were others from the Prijedor municipality, including the court. But I knew the employees of the SUP, such as Obrad Despotovic, Zarko Tejic, Ilija Bijelic, the small Neso and the big Neso. I don't remember their surnames. Lakic was also there. He was from the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you able to -- did you see them or did they speak to you?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No. They didn't know us who were in the camp. They would pass by smiling. They talked to each other, laughed a little, and they would go upstairs to the offices. They never addressed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: On the day that you were brought to the camp, did you see any other prisoners, other than the prisoners -- the people who came with you, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. being brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I saw people being brought there, and I also saw them being taken away in the direction of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people who were brought that day?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Or from which area or from which locality they came from?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: My assumption was that they were people from Carakovo because I learned that on the same morning that I arrived in Omarska, the place of Carakovo was ethnically cleansed, so my assumption was that the people were from Carakovo or the village of Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to them after they came to the camp and before they were taken to the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. As they were being taken by the restaurant, I could see that they were going in the direction of the "white house," and I saw them being beaten up. A man fell down, and then a guard kicked him two times, on his back and in his head. He had a rifle. The man was trying to stand up, but after he had been kicked for the second time he remained laying down, and they simply removed him next to the hedge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies that day?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. I saw corpses when I arrived. I was surprised by that, and I asked one of my colleagues what was going on, and they told me just keep quiet and don't watch. But I started counting the bodies anyway. I watched and watched, and until -- while we were still there, I could count up to 12 dead bodies of the individuals who were lying down on the grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: From where did you see this? Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: At that time I was sitting at the edge of the table, and I had the view of the "white house." I could see it clearly because there were no curtains on the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The next morning, were you asked to come down to the restaurant again?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning we would usually get up at half past 6 or 7.00, I don't remember exactly at what time. We were supposed to prepare the room for the work of the investigators, to remove the mattresses and things like that, and after that we would go downstairs to the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you came down, did you see any bodies?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And were you asked to go upstairs before -- and were not allowed to stay in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And did you know -- did you see or get to know as to what happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: When we went back to the room from the restaurant, we were able to look through the window, and we saw in front of the restaurant and the kitchen yellow dumping trucks pass by carrying bodies. The trucks were fully loaded with corpses. As we were coming down the stairs, we saw this terrible sight. Bodies were all around the place, from the "white house" to the restaurant. The bodies were next to each other, crowded next to each other like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, now you mentioned about some trucks. Did you recognise any of these trucks? Were they the trucks from the mine?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Yes. It was a yellow truck. We called them demper. It's a kind of dumping truck, a small truck. And I saw the truck pass by, although we were not allowed to watch through the window, but of course we were curious and we were trying to see what was going on through the window. And I saw this small yellow truck because very often it would be parked behind the garage, behind the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You mentioned areas as Carakovo and Rizvanovici. Is this -- are these villages called or is this area referred to as Brdo area?

utterances.speaker: Nedzija Fazlic
utterances.text: Those are villages, Carakovo is situated below the hill, and Rizvanovici is on top of the hill. But the village in question was the village of Carakovo and, of course, the village of Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I at this stage request to go into private session as the witness would be testifying with regard to a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday the 11th day of September, 2000, at 9:30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2:45 p.m., to
